The word affair refers to a matter, situation, event, or piece of business — something that is happening, has happened, or needs to be dealt with. Think of it as a general-purpose word that covers a wide range of situations. Because it is so flexible, it has developed several specific meanings over time, depending on the context. Understanding each meaning separately will make this word crystal clear.
Meaning 1: A General Matter or Situation

This is the broadest and most basic meaning. When something happens — especially something complicated, notable, or worth discussing — you can call it "an affair."

"The whole affair was handled very badly."
"It was a messy affair from the beginning."
"Nobody fully understood the affair."

Here, "affair" simply means the situation or the matter at hand. You're not saying what specifically happened — you're speaking about the whole thing as a unit. This is very useful when something is hard to describe in one word, or when you want to speak about it broadly.
Meaning 2: A Social Event or Occasion

"Affair" is frequently used to describe a social gathering or event, especially one that has a particular character — grand, formal, small, quiet, lavish, etc.

"The wedding was a magnificent affair."
"The birthday party was a small, family affair."
"The gala dinner was quite a formal affair."

Notice how this usage almost always comes with a describing word (adjective) in front of it — grand, small, formal, quiet, lavish. That adjective tells you what kind of event it was. "Affair" here is just a sophisticated synonym for event, occasion, or gathering.
Meaning 3: A Romantic or Sexual Relationship Outside a Committed Relationship

This is probably the most well-known specific meaning in modern usage. An affair (often called a love affair or simply an affair) refers to a secret romantic or sexual relationship between two people, where at least one of them is already married or committed to someone else.

"She found out her husband was having an affair."
"He ended the affair before his wife discovered it."
"The affair lasted two years."

The key elements here are:

  • It is romantic or sexual in nature.
  • It is usually secret.
  • It involves a breach of commitment — at least one person is cheating on their partner.

When used without any other context, and especially in everyday conversation, people almost always understand "an affair" to mean this.

Note: The phrase "love affair" can sometimes be used more innocently, to mean a deep passion for something — not necessarily involving a person.

"She had a lifelong love affair with music."

Here, it simply means she was deeply and passionately devoted to music. Context will always make this clear.
Meaning 4: Someone's Personal Business or Concern

When you say something is "someone's affair," you mean it is their own personal business — it concerns them, not you, and others should not interfere.

"What he does with his money is his own affair."
"It's not your affair how I spend my evenings."

This meaning carries a tone of privacy and boundary-setting. You're essentially saying: "This does not concern you." It is often used to politely (or firmly) tell someone to mind their own business.
Meaning 5: Affairs (Plural) — Matters of Business, Life, or Public Concern

When used in the plural form — "affairs" — the word takes on a slightly different flavour. It refers to ongoing matters, responsibilities, or activities in a particular area of life, work, or public life.

In personal life:

"He needed time to sort out his personal affairs."
"She put her affairs in order before leaving the country."

Here, "affairs" means all the things she needed to manage — finances, documents, responsibilities, etc.

In public and political life, "affairs" is commonly used in fixed phrases:

  • Foreign affairs — A country's dealings and relationships with other countries. (Many governments have a "Ministry of Foreign Affairs.")
  • Current affairs — Recent and ongoing events happening in the world, especially in politics and society. (News programmes often cover "current affairs.")
  • Affairs of state — The important matters of running a government or a country.
  • Internal affairs — Matters happening within an organization, country, or institution — not involving outsiders.

"The minister of foreign affairs gave a speech."
"She always kept up with current affairs."

This is a more informal, slightly old-fashioned use. Sometimes, people use "affair" to refer to a physical object or thing, especially when they don't know the exact name for it, or they want to be vague or humorous about it.

"She wore a large, feathered affair on her head." (= some kind of hat)
"The car was a beaten-up, rusty affair." (= a beaten-up, rusty thing)
"He sat on a wooden affair that passed for a chair." (= a rough wooden thing that was being used as a chair)

This usage gives a sense that the speaker is being casual, slightly dismissive, or gently humorous about the object.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Since "affair" has many meanings, context does all the work. Ask yourself:

  • Are people talking about a situation or incident? → Meaning 1 (a matter/situation)
  • Are people talking about a party or gathering? → Meaning 2 (a social event)
  • Are people talking about someone cheating on their partner? → Meaning 3 (romantic relationship outside commitment)
  • Is someone saying something is "your affair" or "not my affair"? → Meaning 4 (personal concern/business)
  • Are people talking about managing life, finances, government, or world events? → Meaning 5 (affairs in the plural/serious matters)
  • Is someone describing a physical object vaguely? → Meaning 6 (informal: a thing)

In every case, the surrounding words and the situation will make the meaning unmistakable.

What makes "affair" a rich word is that it functions as a kind of container word — it holds whatever situation, event, or matter you pour into it. It can be as serious as government policy ("foreign affairs"), as personal as a family event ("a quiet, intimate affair"), or as dramatic as a betrayal ("he had an affair"). Mastering it is less about memorizing definitions and more about recognizing the context in which it appears — and now you are fully equipped to do exactly that.
